claim: Intuition is trustworthy only in a regular environment with learnable cues and feedback; felt confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy.
note: One review (two authors from opposed camps). Supported indirectly by LLM calibration lines b-11 and b-12.

claim: Stated or verbalized LLM confidence is poorly calibrated; sample consistency helps a little; failure prediction from confidence is weak (AUROC about 0.52-0.61).
note: Same study. Consistent with Kahneman and Klein on humans. Supports gating on agreement and checks, not stated confidence.

claim: Simple mechanical or formula prediction beats clinical judgment on average (about 10% accuracy), with experts clearly better in only 6-16% of studies.
note: One meta-analysis. The two lines give 6-16% and 33-47% for different tails; not a contradiction. Transfer: prefer a checker or rule over judgment when one exists.

claim: Einstellung: a familiar good-but-not-best solution blocks a better one, even in experts, and the effect shrinks when the familiar move is a blunder.
note: Bilalic 2008 and Sheridan-Reingold 2013 are separate experiments (a-06 and c-12 are the same paper). Chess only. Supports gating forced divergence to open tasks.

claim: LLMs show Einstellung-like anchoring: on 5,383 paired medical cases with flipped evidence, frontier models have severe bias-trap rates.
note: Single preprint, low credibility. The earlier brief's 60.9% figure is NOT in the abstract (b-02); drop it.

claim: Chess expertise is a large library of chunks and templates; the memory edge persists even for random material (moderate correlation), so it is not only meaningful-pattern recall.
note: Sala-Gobet 2017 meta-analysis and Gobet-Simon 1996. Qualifies the older claim that the edge vanishes on random positions. Domain-specific.

claim: Deliberate practice explains much of performance variance in games (26%), less elsewhere (under 1% in professions); expertise gains are domain-dependent.
note: One meta-analysis, contested by the deliberate-practice camp (not fetched). Weak relevance to agent design.

claim: A feeling of rightness from the fast answer, driven by fluency, predicts whether people rethink; low feeling leads to more rethinking and answer changes.
note: Same experiments. A machine analogue (agreement across samples) is untested in our data.

claim: Reasoning is better at evaluating others' arguments than producing one's own; solitary reasoning is biased toward supporting existing views.
note: Theory paper with heavy commentary; both lines are the same source. Not an experiment.

claim: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback; accuracy sometimes drops.
note: Huang 2024, Kamoi 2024 survey and Stechly 2023/24 are independent. The survey allows exceptions for well-suited tasks. A sound external verifier gives large gains (c-03).

claim: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or a single strong prompt at matched cost; much of the gain looks like extra sampling.
note: Smit 2023, Wang 2024 and Cemri 2025 against Du 2023's original gains. Du's gains are real on its tasks; the dispute is about cause. Some variants improve with tuning.

claim: Self-consistency (sample many paths, take the majority) improves over greedy chain of thought, e.g. GSM8K +17.9.
note: Original paper only in this set. Caveat: errors are correlated (see b-10).

claim: LLMs prefer their own outputs when judging, and self-recognition drives self-preference.
note: Three lines, one paper. No independent replication fetched. Supports hiding authorship in critic steps.

claim: Errors across LLMs are highly correlated: when two models are both wrong they give the same wrong answer about 60% of the time; larger, more accurate models are more correlated.
note: One 350+ model study. Supports our own finding that agreement is weak evidence.

claim: Chain of thought helps mainly on math and symbolic or logic tasks and little elsewhere.
note: b-15 and c-09 are the same meta-analysis (Sprague et al.). Do not count as two.

claim: Chain of thought can lower accuracy on tasks where deliberation also hurts humans (up to 36.3 points for o1-preview vs GPT-4o on one task).
note: Preprint. Matches our word-puzzle drop. The 36% in c-10 is a different effect (biased context).

claim: Chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful: biasing context cut accuracy by up to 36% and models rationalized wrong answers.
note: Same paper counted twice. Implication: a written rationale is not proof of the real reason; require a run or check.

claim: Newer chat models avoid human-like intuitive errors on cognitive reflection tasks and stay accurate even when chain of thought is blocked, so fast and slow are entangled in models.
note: One paper counted four times. Figures in b-13 and c-14 are worded differently (c-14 text is truncated); check the paper tables before quoting.

claim: Compositional multi-step tasks degrade fast as complexity grows because transformers match subgraphs rather than compose reliably.
note: One experiment; not tied to a particular agent step.

claim: Ensembled LLMs match a human crowd at forecasting, and showing models the human median forecast raises accuracy 17-28%.
note: 31 questions only. Suggests an outside-view anchor in open forecasting tasks.

claim: Pre-mortem raises the quantity of reasons generated, but no controlled study shows better final decisions; the 30% figure counts reasons, not quality.
note: Mostly snippets or a conceptual review; the 1989 paper and Veinott 2010 were not opened. Evidence for the pre-mortem step is thin, not refuted.

claim: Pre-execution critique of a plan, using errors distilled from past trajectories, improves agent utility over reflection after failure.
note: Preprint, credibility 45; abstract only.

claim: Larger LLMs reason more logically on syllogisms than humans but keep human-like systematic biases, and LLMs apply rules too rigidly where common sense blocks a valid conclusion.
note: Two independent studies (Eisape 2023, Chan 2025), both abstract level. No result that a counterexample-search step improves accuracy.

claim: A transformer trained on engine values reaches grandmaster-level chess with no explicit search, so pattern knowledge can replace search.
note: Preprint. Not a prompting method.

claim: Tetlock: foxes forecast better than hedgehogs.
note: Only a commentary snippet; the book was not opened. Treat as memory-level.
